desc:
For every level of a binary tree, compute the average of the values of its nodes, rounded down to an integer. Return these averages from the top level to the bottom level. The empty tree gives [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [3, 9, 20, -1, -1, 15, 7] the levels are [3], [9, 20] and [15, 7], with exact averages 3, 14.5 and 11, so the answer is [3, 14, 11].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Each level needs two numbers: the sum of its values and the count of its nodes.
Because the array is in level order, a node's level is one more than its parent's level. Keep a depth per node and two parallel lists sums and counts indexed by depth.
At the end the average of level d is sums[d] // counts[d]. All values are non-negative, so integer division rounds down.
editorial: Group the values by level (a breadth-first search, or a single pass over the array that propagates depths from parents to children) while keeping only a running sum and a node count for each level. After the pass, divide each sum by its count with floor division.
No floating point numbers are needed, which also removes any rounding doubt. Time is linear in the number of nodes and the extra space is proportional to the number of levels (plus the depth array).
